newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Brady swap seeks to dodge Mexico quirks.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Brady swap seeks to dodge Mexico quirks.

text.p: Brazilian debt watchers said the government's offer to buy back Brady bonds or swap them for a new 30-year global issue was structured to avoid some of the problems Mexico ran into last year with its landmark deal.

"In addition to the swap, Brazil is offering a formal buyback and a straight purchase of the new bond, which you didn't have with Mexico," said Pedro Barbosa, head of Brady trading at ING Barings in Brazil.
"So this basically opens it up to non-Brady holders too," Barbosa added.
Although Mexico's unprecedented May 1, 1996 deal was widely regarded as a success, its simplicity led to some pricing problems ahead of the exchange.

Namely, the deal required investors to exchange Bradys for the new 30-year global bond, forcing non-Brady holders wanting to participate in the new deal to buy Bradys. This drove Mexican Brady prices up well beyond the tender price set by the government.
Four days before the April 30 deadline to submit bids for the swap offering, Mexico was forced to alter the tender price to keep the deal attractive.

"In the Mexico case the deal was much more simple. But its simplicity gave rise to arbitrage in the market. Brazil does not want anybody arbitraging in the market other than itself," said Tina Vandersteel, a fixed-income analyst at J.P. Morgan in Brazil.
J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs are coordinating the deal, which was announced Wednesday in New York.
Investors have three options under the plan. First, holders of Brazil Par bonds, C bonds and Discount Z-L bonds may exchange their instruments for a newly issued 30-year global bond.

Second, investors can offer to sell their Pars and Discounts for cash, but the total may not exceed 25 percent of the total Pars and Discounts in the swap. Finally, investors can buy the global bond for cash, but only 25 percent of the total new issue can be sold this way.
The offer expires June 3, and results will be announced the following day.

As far as the swap option goes, market players said exchanging Pars and Discounts would be attractive because trading U.S. Treasury backed Bradys for the uncollateralized global bond would give investors a decent yield pickup.

But exchanging uncollateralized Cs, which come due in 2014, for the uncollateralized global, which would come due in 2027, is essentially asking investors to extend their risk with no significant yield pickup, traders and analysts said.

"There is a consensus that C bonds are the worst to be traded in the swap. So far, most of our clients are interested in a direct cash purchase of the global," said a trader at a leading Brazilian investment bank.
Also investors were not seen rushing to unload their Bradys through the direct buyback option because the market looked well supported in the short term, traders said.

The size of the global would depend on demand, with the market talking about a range of between $1 billion and $4 billion. Brazil, which has $26 billion in outstanding Brady debt, has set no limit on the offer.

The global was expected to price somewhere between 370 to 400 basis points over the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond. But some market players said it could drop to 350 bp over, barring any negative news on the political front between now and June 3.
"None of the big houses want to miss out on this deal so they are going to come in bidding at low spreads to guarantee they get something," said one debt trader in Sao Paulo.
